## Drew's ask (2026-11-12)

Do we have SSO for our own fleet services shaped like this — and if not, this issue is its home:

1. **Accept external login, gated to Drew (for now):** sign in with **GitHub**, **Google**, or **Microsoft** — allowlisted to Drew's accounts only.
2. **Our own OAuth/OIDC provider:** stand up a devtoday identity provider usable by ANY of our apps, with **basic roles**, offered to our apps as a **"devtoday SSO"** button — the same way apps offer "Sign in with Google".
3. **Account linking:** one account, every door. GitHub / Google / Microsoft / the devtoday provider are all linkable to the SAME account at the user's choice, so a single account accepts any of the options interchangeably.

## What already exists (evidence, 2026-11-12 search)

- **#1182** — dashboard behind Cloudflare Access, identity = Drew's Google SSO. Covers a slice of (1) for ONE app via Cloudflare Access (Google only), and is explicitly gated on Drew's go, not yet implemented.
- **#1253** — design: one identity across the PM stack, SSO propagation from the public entry into every layer, roles (owner / orchestrator / agent / read-only) replacing asserted authorship. Assumes an IdP at the entry (Cloudflare Access); does NOT stand up our own provider, name GitHub/Microsoft as login options, or specify account linking.
- **#2852 / spec #2258** (ID program, epic #2056) — hosted provisioning + **SSO→ID binding**: external SSO identities bound to pkgs/id accounts; slices 1–2 landed (PRs #4854, #4885), slices 3–4 open. This is linking INSIDE the id system; it does not make any fleet service accept those logins, and id is not (yet) cast as an OIDC issuer for other apps.
- pkgs/id itself (epic #2056) is Drew's identity system — capabilities (id-caps), directory, groups; production node on the laptop :3005; a Cloudflare Workers "serverless edition" is designed/implemented under #5524 / #5681. Related login-design line: #5684 (identity, login & delegation), #5885, #5889.
- No issue found (searches: oidc, oauth, sso, "identity provider", "login with", "relying party", "devtoday") that frames (1)+(2)+(3) together for fleet services, and none that offers a "devtoday SSO" button to our own apps.

## Open design question (for the owner — NOT decided here)

**Is pkgs/id the OIDC provider, or a separate minimal provider?**
- For id-as-provider: it already has accounts, binding ceremonies (#2852), capability/role machinery (id-caps, id-groups), a hosted/serverless edition path (#5524), and Drew's 2026-10-28 ID program directive behind it. Cost: id's key-custody model (see #5684) is more exotic than a conventional OIDC issuer; fleet services need boring, standard OIDC first.
- For a separate minimal provider: a small standard OIDC issuer (GitHub/Google/Microsoft as upstream federated logins + linking tables + roles) is faster to make every app consume, but then two identity systems exist and the relationship (does the minimal provider later fold into id? does id consume it?) must be designed, not drifted into.
Either way the deliverables above stand: external logins gated to Drew, account linking across all four doors, basic roles consumed by fleet services (the role model in #1253 is the consumer-side contract).

## Acceptance

- A design note (repo `doc/`) answering the provider question above with evidence, naming the issuer, the linking model (one account, N linked external identities), the role set, and the Drew-only gate mechanism.
- Implementation issues filed as children of this issue for: provider stand-up, GitHub login, Google login, Microsoft login, account linking UI/flow, first consumer integration (PM stack, per #1253).
- First consumer proves the full loop: Drew signs into a fleet service via each linked door against the same account, roles enforced server-side.

Parents/relatives: PM stack coherence epic #1184 (this issue's native parent), ID program epic #2056 (cross-linked — the provider question lives there too), design-register/turso-cloudflare programs unaffected. Relates: #1182, #1253, #2852, #2258, #5684, #5524.

## Program (Drew's directive, 2026-11-12 16:58 CST)

The PM stack and pkgs/id cannot run on Cloudflare Workers today. Build **workable equivalents** of the PM service, the ID service, and the fleet tool for the Workers world, on a multi-tenant data architecture. This is a large multi-part design program: it runs through the **design mill** — this epic is the starter issue; the design is produced by a summit session owning the queue item for this epic, in the mill pattern (statement inventory → state-of-the-art expansion → versioned designs → granular implementation issues). Component issues A–H below carry the open design questions; the mill's designs answer them and spawn the granular implementation issues.

Drew's sketch, in substance:

- **Per-user ID databases in Turso** plus a **central tenancy database**, handled and served by Workers and Durable Objects. Hosted per-user instances connect and sync their data; everyone can also connect to a large **public database** we offer.
- **Media/content plane:** media content-addressed and deduped in **R2**, with sensitivity tiers deciding placement and access (R2 + access controls, CDN for public content, or inside the Turso DB where that fits). Central open question (posed, not decided): because everything is Turso/Cloudflare, maybe data is **not copied into each DB** — a DB holds IDs/references and the content lives once in R2, garbage-collectable only when **all** references drop; a user may access an object iff their DB holds a reference to it, or it is public-published in one or more DBs. Copy-into-each-DB and hybrid models are evaluated against this sketch.
- **Transports:** Workers limitations mean this is substantially a **second version in TypeScript** — the design says so plainly and scopes it. Client-side **WASM** is allowed in selected areas (evaluate per component what Rust logic — e.g. ID crypto/store logic — compiles to WASM vs must be rewritten). All base functions must work over **REST or WebSocket** transports (HTTP/2/3, QUIC where the platform provides it). **Direct Turso access** to the user's own DB and to the public DB is also allowed when prudent, under the tenancy/auth rules.
- **ID data stores:** ID gains **Turso/SQLite-over-HTTP as a database store in addition to redb**, and **IndexedDB** is evaluated for the browser client — one storage interface, pluggable backends.
- **Identity:** the hosted services are relying parties for #9077 (GitHub/Google/Microsoft login gated to Drew + devtoday OIDC provider with roles + account linking); the tenancy account model lines up with #9077/#1253's roles. Identity itself is NOT re-designed here.

## Components (each its own issue under this epic)

- **A.** PM service, Workers edition — TypeScript equivalent of aggregator/dashboard/reconcile as one hosted service.
- **B.** ID service, Workers edition — the missing pieces on top of the existing serverless line (#5524, #5681, #3811).
- **C.** Fleet tool, Workers/TypeScript equivalent — hosted Metadata stamping/query, session provenance, sync tools.
- **D.** ID store abstraction — Turso/SQLite-over-HTTP beside redb; IndexedDB evaluated.
- **E.** Tenancy architecture — per-user Turso DBs + central tenancy DB; Workers/DO serving; public DB.
- **F.** Content-addressed media/data plane — R2 dedup, reference-based access, GC on last reference.
- **G.** Second-version-in-TypeScript scoping + transports — REST/WebSocket everywhere, WASM where it fits, direct Turso when prudent.
- **H.** SSO relying-party integration — hosted services consume #9077; tenancy accounts ↔ #1253 roles.

## Lineage and relations

- Data model consumed, not re-invented: #9060's merged design (doc/2026-11-12T22-50-00Z_design_pm-board-hierarchy-genealogy) — board registry, hierarchy, Metadata. Children #9062 (collector registry), #9070 (genealogy read model), #9073/#9074 (fleet Metadata superset + metadata DB), #9076 (dual ingestion) are the laptop-world counterparts this program's hosted editions must stay model-compatible with.
- Turso + Cloudflare epic: #8987. PM data unification background: #3142, #1744. Fleet sync tools: #9016. SSO: #9077, #1253, #2852. ID program: #2056.

## Acceptance (program level)

- [ ] Design-mill build-out complete: statement inventory covering A–H with zero unmapped statements; versioned designs (V1 = what exists today) merged to main under doc/.
- [ ] Every component issue's named open questions answered in a merged design or explicitly batched to Drew as a ruling with options + recommendation.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed for everything implementable, parented under the component issues.
- [ ] The F-plane reference-vs-copy question decided with evidence (or batched to Drew with a recommendation).

Component **D** of epic #9078 (hosted editions program) — Drew's explicit item (2026-11-12). Design first (design mill, under #9078); filed under the ID program because the store is pkgs/id's own layer.

## What

One storage interface for pkgs/id with pluggable backends:

- **redb** — the existing native backend (stays).
- **Turso / SQLite-over-HTTP (libSQL)** — NEW backend, so the same ID store runs against a hosted per-user Turso DB (component E of #9078) or the public DB.
- **IndexedDB** — EVALUATE for the browser client (offline/local-first web use); adopt, defer, or reject with evidence.

- #5681 (serverless storage: D1 vs Turso vs both) and #5863 (serverless storage contract) cover the SERVERLESS EDITION's storage choice — this issue is the store layer of id itself, shared by native, hosted, and browser builds. Coordinate: the contract in #5863 and the interface here must not diverge silently; divergences are named in the design.
- Consumers: component B (hosted ID) and component E (per-user Turso DBs) under #9078; ID epic #2056.

## Open design questions

1. Interface shape: what is the smallest store contract (get/put/delete/scan/transactions/watch?) that redb, libSQL-over-HTTP, and IndexedDB can ALL honor without leaking backend semantics — and what id features (event store, group log) stress it hardest?

3. Which backend is authoritative in each deployment shape (native single-user, hosted per-user, browser) and how does sync/migration between backends work (redb → Turso lift for existing users)?
4. WASM angle: does any backend run as Rust-compiled WASM in the browser (redb on WASM? libSQL WASM client?) vs TypeScript implementations — feeds component G of #9078.

Component **E** of epic #9078 (hosted editions program). Design first (design mill, under #9078).

## What (Drew's sketch, 2026-11-12)

- **Per-user ID databases in Turso**: each user gets their own hosted database(s), served and handled by Workers and Durable Objects (routing, auth, sync coordination, provisioning).
- A **central tenancy database**: the registry of users, their databases, account state, and roles — the control plane the Workers consult.
- **Hosted per-user instances connect and sync their data** (a user's local/native instance ↔ their hosted DB, both directions, with a conflict story).
- A large **public database we offer**: everyone can connect to it too — public content published there is readable by all; how publishing works (component F's reference model) is designed with F.

## Builds on / relations

- #3811 — hosted Worker API + per-user DO provisioning and metering (the closest existing machinery; E must state whether it builds on, wraps, or supersedes it).
- Turso + Cloudflare epic: #8987 (databases, edge, scoped credentials). Identity/accounts: #9077 + component H under #9078; roles from #1253. Store backends: component D. Blob jurisdiction isolation: #3401.

## Open design questions

1. Tenancy DB schema: what lives centrally (accounts, DB registry, roles, publish index?) vs per-user — and what must NEVER live centrally (content? keys?)?
2. DO responsibilities: one DO per user? per DB? — routing, presence, sync sessions, rate limiting, metering (vs #3811's metering).
3. Provisioning lifecycle: signup → tenancy row → Turso DB creation → credential issuance/rotation → suspension/deletion; who can do each step.
4. Sync protocol: native instance ↔ hosted DB — change capture, ordering, conflict resolution, offline behavior; does sync ride component G's transports or direct Turso replication?
5. Public DB: single shared Turso DB or a federation — write path (who may publish), moderation/abuse controls, and how per-user DBs reference its content (component F).
6. Credential model for direct Turso access (component G): scoped, expiring tokens per user per DB — issuance and revocation from the tenancy plane.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under doc/ as part of #9078's build-out: tenancy schema sketch, DO inventory, provisioning lifecycle, sync protocol, public-DB rules.
- [ ] Relationship to #3811 decided and recorded.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed under this issue.

Component **F** of epic #9078 (hosted editions program). Design first (design mill, under #9078). This carries the program's CENTRAL open question.

## Drew's sketch (posed, not decided — 2026-11-12)

Media is **content-addressed and deduped in R2**. Sensitivity tiers decide placement and access: R2 with access controls, CDN for public content, or inside the Turso DB where that fits.

Because everything is already Turso/Cloudflare, maybe data does NOT need to be copied into each database: **the DB holds IDs/references; the content lives once in R2** and can be garbage-collected only when ALL references drop. Access rule candidate: a user may access an object iff their DB holds a reference to it, OR the object is public-published in one or more DBs.

## Alternatives the design must evaluate against the sketch

1. Reference-only (Drew's sketch above).
2. Copy-into-each-DB (content replicated per tenant DB).
3. Hybrid (small content inline in DB, large content referenced in R2; or hot/cold split by sensitivity/size).

Evaluation axes: storage cost under dedup, access-control soundness (can a reference be forged or enumerated?), GC correctness (reference counting vs mark-and-sweep across many DBs; races with new references), deletion/privacy (a user deleting content others still reference; jurisdiction rules per #3401), latency (extra hop through R2 vs local rows), and what 'published public' means mechanically.

## Builds on / relations

- Tenancy: component E under #9078 (per-user DBs + public DB are where references live). Turso + Cloudflare epic: #8987 (R2, CDN).
- #3401 — isolate hosted blobs by jurisdiction and minimize shared directory (ID hosted blobs; the sensitivity/jurisdiction input).
- Atlas's content-addressed provenance work (#3125) is a DIFFERENT domain — prior art to consult, not a dependency.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under doc/ as part of #9078's build-out: the three models compared on the axes above; a recommendation recorded — decided in the mill or batched to Drew with options + recommendation.
- [ ] Sensitivity tier table: which content classes go R2-private / R2 + CDN / in-DB, and the access check for each.

Component **G** of epic #9078 (hosted editions program). Design first (design mill, under #9078). This is the program's cross-cutting runtime/transport design; components A–C consume its verdicts.

## Premise (Drew, 2026-11-12)

Workers limitations mean the hosted editions are substantially **a second version written in TypeScript**. The design says so plainly and scopes exactly what 'second version' covers — PM service (A), ID service (B), fleet tool (C) — and what is NOT rewritten.

## Scope of the design

1. **Rewrite-vs-WASM per component**: client-side WASM is allowed in selected areas. For each piece of Rust logic (ID crypto and store logic are the named candidates), evaluate: compile to WASM and reuse / rewrite in TypeScript / keep server-side only. Criteria: correctness risk (crypto!), maintenance divergence between two implementations of the same semantics, bundle/runtime limits.
2. **Transports**: ALL base functions must work over REST or WebSocket transports (HTTP/2/3, QUIC where the platform provides it). Define the base-function inventory per component and the transport contract for each (request/response vs streaming vs realtime sync), including offline/reconnect behavior.
3. **Direct Turso access**: also allowed — to the user's OWN database and to the PUBLIC database — 'when prudent'. This design defines prudent: which operations may go direct (reads? writes? sync?), under what credential scoping/expiry (from component E), and which operations must NEVER bypass the service layer (anything needing stamping, authorization beyond the DB scope, or cross-tenant access).
4. **Shared-semantics discipline**: how the TS version and the Rust/native version keep one data model (Metadata, packets, store contracts) — shared schemas/fixtures/tests, and what happens when they diverge.

## Builds on / relations

- Components A, B, C, D, E under #9078 (D's WASM question feeds §1; E's credential model feeds §3).
- #5671 — ID transport fallback for UDP-denied networks (transport prior art inside the ID program).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under doc/ as part of #9078's build-out: per-component rewrite/WASM table, base-function transport inventory, direct-Turso prudence rules.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed under this issue or handed to the owning component issues with cross-links.

Design-mill starter for the **Atlas v1 program** (Drew directive, 2026-11-12 17:38 CST): build out a full design for a strong v1 of Atlas — search build-out with Workers fan-out, the backup mesh, the Metadata schema + evolution doctrine, the per-embed classification model, always-on corpus ingestion, embed-storage economics, query-as-data, a virtual filesystem over the content-addressed store, and the worker-instructions rollout.

## Workstream A — Search subcommand build-out + Workers fan-out

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design: `doc/2026-11-12T23-59-00Z_design_atlas_v1_proto/note.md` §A · Starter: the Atlas v1 design-mill starter issue (sibling).

### Current state (verified 2026-11-12)

`atlas-search` / `fleet search`: one-stage hybrid (FTS5/BM25 + Snowflake cosine, RRF k=10) over a 7.3 GB Turso monolith (107,639 chunks) + 29 topic shards. The shard fan-out path is a hidden experimental flag (`--shards`, #5755); the production default is the monolith scan. Contract flags for the query planner, spell correction, query-class hint, and `rewritten|both` variants are **accepted but unimplemented**. The Cloudflare Worker cache (one Durable Object per query key) caches results **indefinitely — no TTL, eviction, or invalidation** (#6805 open; gated purge route #8312). No result caching in the standalone CLI (#5668). Query-understanding front-end and parameter surface are open designs #5773/#5774.

### Scope

1. **Search v1 build-out:** implement the dead contract surface or formally retire each flag — planner (query understanding per #5773), spell, query-class hint, rewritten/both variants; Jaccard third signal per #5733 where it earns its place. Every advertised flag either works or is removed from the contract.
2. **Workers fan-out:** make the hosted search path fan out across Workers/Durable Objects/shards as the default serving shape: parallel shard queries, connection fan-out, DO roles (coordination, hot shards, cache). Respect platform limits in the design (Paid: 1,000 subrequests/invocation; DO SQLite 10 GB/object) — wider fan-out chains via queues/multiple invocations.
3. **Shard-size benchmark programme (own deliverable):** benchmark latency vs shard size and shard count across Turso shards AND D1, on the production corpus shape. **Named oracle:** p50/p95 end-to-end query latency at fixed recall@10 against the standing eval sets (#8627) — a shard configuration wins only at equal-or-better recall. Output: a measured shard-size recommendation + the fan-out width curve (where more parallelism stops helping).
4. **Cache policy:** results cached until the corpus changes; on corpus change, cached results may serve for a short, specified staleness window UNLESS the caller passes a real-time requirement or a cache-disable flag (both become first-class search flags, in the CLI, the service protocol, and the Worker). Builds on #6805's eviction/invalidation policy and #8312's purge route; the corpus-change signal (ingest watermark) is defined with workstream E.
5. **Second embedder:** evaluate a second embedding approach alongside Snowflake arctic-embed-m-v2.0 (candidates to evaluate, not pre-picked: BGE-M3, Voyage, OpenAI text-embedding-3, Workers AI models — judged on quality vs the eval sets, cost, self-hostability, and mixed-embedder corpus support under the workstream C schema). Per-corpus model identity already exists as a concept (#8623); v1 must support mixed embedders in one corpus without a flag-day re-embed.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Design doc(s) merged under `doc/` covering items 1–5, with the benchmark programme's protocol (corpus snapshot, query set, oracle) specified before any benchmark runs.
- [ ] Benchmark results published in the design or a linked research doc: latency/recall table per shard size × count, Turso and D1, with the chosen configuration named.
- [ ] Cache semantics specified exactly: invalidation trigger, staleness window value, real-time + cache-disable flag names and behavior at every surface (CLI/service/Worker).
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed for each build item; dead-flag disposition (implement vs retire) recorded per flag.

## Workstream H — Virtual filesystem over the content-addressed store

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design §H · **References, does not restate:** #9084 (content plane: addressing, GC, sensitivity tiers — the store this filesystem sits on) and #3125 (Atlas provenance/occurrence registry — in-domain prior art; the occurrence registry is this design's closest ancestor).

### The model (Drew, 2026-11-12)

- Content lands **content-addressed and immutable**: bytes are uploaded once and never change.
- **Paths are a first-class abstraction over the bytes** — a rough virtual filesystem. "Find everything referencing `geordi.png`" returns every path/location naming those bytes, across hosts and stores.
- The same bytes in five places = **one upload + five metadata records**. Each location record carries its own metadata: the path, the host it came from, the date, the process that produced/placed it — attached as metadata on the embeds/records for that location.
- Locations are editable/addable without touching the bytes: adding a sixth place that references the same content adds a metadata record, nothing else.

### Aggregated index (the performance rule)

Byte-hash and filename lookups must **not** scan the whole Atlas corpus's metadata. The virtual-file index is **aggregated**: its own Turso database, or dedicated tables maintained beside the bucket (a sidecar manifest/index uploaded alongside the content-addressed data so the bucket works standalone), with lookups by hash, by filename, by path prefix, and by host.

### Big-data evaluation (required, not optional)

Evaluate whether the aggregated metadata belongs in a big-data system instead of / beside the Turso index:

- **Parquet** (file-format lake over R2),
- **Cloudflare Basin** (verified: GA 2026-10-01; the renamed Cloudflare Data Platform — Apache Iceberg over R2: Basin Pipelines for ingest, Basin Catalog for table maintenance, Basin SQL for serverless queries over Iceberg tables; an analytics/lakehouse fit, not a transactional store),
- or another system the research surfaces — judged on lookup latency for the VFS query shapes (hash, filename, prefix), update cost under constant ingestion (workstream E), and operational weight.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Design merged under `doc/`: the location-record schema (aligned with workstream C doctrine), the aggregated index shape, and the VFS query set (by hash, filename, path, host) with latency expectations.
- [ ] The big-data evaluation published with a verdict (Turso index / Parquet / Basin / hybrid) and its evidence.
- [ ] Worked example in the design: one image at five locations — records, lookups, and what a rename/move/deletion of one location does (and does not do) to the others.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed; #9084 and #3125 cross-linked from the design.

# Program: ID/Atlas extensible primitives, federation, namespaces

**Source:** Drew directive, 2026-11-12 18:29 CST (clarifies and greatly extends the hosted-editions program #9078). Filed via design-mill intake; the summit elaboration is queued as a design-mill task pointing at this issue.

## What this program is

A new major design iteration for the ID substrate and its Atlas-facing surfaces, in three parts:

- **Part A — ID core** (namespaces, ID shapes, triples, user attributes): the addressing and data model everything else stands on.
- **Part B — federation & trust**: how peer servers exchange signed data, sync, fan out queries, and earn or lose trust.
- **Part C — Atlas-facing economics & discovery**: storage benchmarks/economics, ID search, recommendations.

Program-level items (§0 extensibility architecture, §7 modes/configuration, refine-and-prioritize) sit directly under this epic.

**Why three parts, not one flat list:** the directive itself splits this way — one part Atlas, one part ID, one part the federation layer both share. The parts have different design tempos (Part A is data model, Part B is protocol/trust, Part C is measurement-driven) and different nearest neighbors (#2056 ID designs; #9083 tenancy; #8983 Atlas). One program epic keeps the statement inventory whole: nothing in the directive belongs to only one audience, and the summit owns cohesion across the parts.

## Clarification of record (§0)

Extensibility IS the architecture goal. Primitives, adapters, and hooks are **designed** for the full matrix of stores / buckets / streams / transports from the start. What was de-prioritized in #9078/#9082's framing is **implementing** the long tail now — the earlier "plumbing, not a matrix" line stands as an implementation priority, NOT as an architecture limit. Both tier-1 editions (Rust binaries, Cloudflare/Turso hosted) are fully featured; neither is a reduced edition. Everything behavioral is configuration where it is behavior, primitives where it is mechanism (§7). Our system is not special: every capability is a config option anyone could replicate by investing the same effort.

## Inputs / feeds

- Feeds into and amends: #9078 (hosted editions), #9082 (store abstraction), #9083 (tenancy), #9084 (content plane), #9085 (TS transports), Atlas starter #9091 and VFS #9100, ID epic #2056 (parent).
- Proto design scaffold: `doc/` note merged with this intake (linked below once merged).
- Statement inventory: numbered S0–S7 in the proto design; every statement maps to a component issue under this epic or to a named existing issue. Zero unmapped is the intake acceptance bar; the summit verifies it again (mill return-on-agreement).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Statement inventory verified complete by the summit + a fresh judge pass (zero unmapped).
- [ ] Versioned designs (V1 = what exists today; V2+ layer the vision) merged under `doc/` for each part, or the part explicitly folded into an existing design by amendment with the link recorded here.
- [ ] Granular implementation issues filed under the component issues for everything implementable.
- [ ] Open questions batched to Drew with options + a recommendation; defaults recorded, never stalled on.
